title: Kuwait Destroys Iranian Drones as Trump Vows to 'Keep Winning' Amid Gulf Escalation
excerpt: Kuwait's military intercepts drones targeting vital installations while UKMTO reports tanker strikes near Oman, as the five-month US-Iran conflict shows no signs of abating.
body:
• Kuwait's military shot down Iranian drones targeting vital and military sites, with falling debris causing property damage but no casualties
  • Two tankers struck near the Strait of Hormuz on August 1, with one left unable to manoeuvre after engine room damage
  • Trump warned the fighting would continue, saying Iran would eventually "peter out" as U.S. strikes degrade its capabilities
  • Oil prices logged their strongest monthly gains since March, with Brent rising 24% in July to above $90 a barrel

Kuwait's armed forces destroyed Iranian drones targeting vital and military installations on Friday, the defence ministry said, as the five-month-old U.S.-Iran war continues to batter the Gulf emirate despite repeated ceasefire attempts.

The Kuwaiti military said interceptor systems neutralised the incoming threats, though falling debris caused material damage to civilian property. No casualties were reported. Iran's army said the strikes were part of its retaliatory campaign against U.S. military facilities hosted in Kuwait, citing a recent American attack on a residence on Qeshm Island near the Strait of Hormuz.

"Countries that are involved in helping the aggressor, if they do not correct their behavior, will receive a harsh response."

— Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps statement, via Tasnim News Agency

Tanker Strikes Signal Fresh Maritime Threat

The escalation on land was mirrored at sea. Britain's UKMTO maritime security agency reported on August 1 that a tanker was struck by an unknown projectile 11 nautical miles northeast of Limah, Oman, sustaining engine room damage that left the vessel unable to manoeuvre. A second tanker reported a large explosion in close proximity 21 nautical miles northeast of Khasab roughly three hours later. No casualties or environmental damage were reported in either incident.

The maritime attacks came as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — which carried roughly a fifth of global oil and gas before the war — fell to a trickle. Kpler tracking data showed just five vessels transiting on July 30, down from 22 the previous day. Iran's Revolutionary Guards also claimed to have stopped two tankers from exiting the strait, while four others reportedly turned back.

Trump Shifts From Diplomacy to Escalation

U.S. President Donald Trump struck an increasingly combative tone on Friday, telling reporters at Camp David that the conflict could drag on but that Iran would "get weaker" over time.

"They'll get weaker. They'll get a little stronger, maybe. But they'll get weaker, and then they peter out."

— Donald Trump, at a Cabinet meeting at Camp David

The remarks marked a sharp reversal from just days earlier, when Trump said the U.S. was having "good talks" with Tehran and saw a "good chance" of a deal. He said Friday that he was "losing faith" in negotiations, accusing Iran of lying.

U.S. Central Command resumed strikes on Iranian targets on July 29 after a brief pause, hitting military command centres, drone storage facilities, and coastal defences. In a first for the war, Saudi Arabia publicly joined U.S. forces in striking Iran-backed groups in eastern Iraq on July 28-29.

Kuwait Caught in the Crossfire

Kuwait, a wealthy oil emirate roughly the size of New Jersey, has borne a disproportionate share of Iran's retaliatory campaign since the war began on February 28. Tehran has pummelled the country with hundreds of missiles and drones, targeting its power and desalination plants, international airport, and Gulf port.

An Indian national was among those killed when Iranian drones struck Kuwait International Airport's Terminal 1 in June, injuring 63 others and forcing the facility to shut down for weeks. The attack prompted Kuwait to expel two Iranian diplomats and summon Tehran's top envoy.

The continued strikes pose particular risks for the estimated one million Indian expatriates in Kuwait, one of the largest diaspora communities in the Gulf. India's External Affairs Ministry has urged Indian nationals in the region to remain vigilant and register with local embassies.

What's Next

Oil prices settled above $90 a barrel on July 31, with Brent logging a 24% gain for July — its strongest monthly performance since March. Analysts polled by Reuters expect prices to climb further as the conflict shows no signs of resolution.

Diplomatic efforts led by Oman, Qatar, Pakistan, and Egypt to revive a June agreement have stalled over control of the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions relief, and Iran's nuclear programme. Iran rejected an Omani proposal for joint management of the strait, insisting on sole control of key shipping channels.

With midterm elections approaching in November, Trump faces mounting pressure to explain when and how the war will end. For now, the administration appears to be settling into a pattern of tit-for-tat strikes with no clear off-ramp — leaving Gulf states and the millions who live in them, including large South Asian communities, in an increasingly precarious position.
image_caption: The Strait of Hormuz, where recent tanker strikes have escalated tensions amid the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict.
nri_angle: Over one million Indian expatriates in Kuwait face continued security risks as Iranian drone and missile strikes hit civilian infrastructure across the emirate.
